keyVerseText: And the angel of the LORD said unto him, Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret ? secret: or, wonderful
rootMeaning: The root of פִּלְאִי (pilʼîy) derives from the Hebrew root פָּלָא (pâlâʼ), which conveys the idea of accomplishing or performing something marvelous, wondrous, or extraordinary. This root suggests a sense of separation or distinction, emphasizing that what is described by פִּלְאִי is not only remarkable but also hidden or beyond ordinary comprehension. Thus, the root meaning adds depth to the English glosses 'secret' and 'wonderful,' highlighting both the mysterious and extraordinary nature of the concept.
usageInScripture: The word פִּלְאִי appears twice in Scripture and is consistently translated with nuances of secrecy and wonder, as seen in the top translations 'seeing it is secret' and 'is too wonderful.' This shows that the term carries a dual sense of something being both hidden and incomprehensible, as well as remarkable or extraordinary. Its usage reveals a consistent theme of divine mystery and awe-inspiring character that resists full human understanding.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding פִּלְאִי enriches our grasp of God's nature as both transcendent and inscrutable. The word underscores that God's ways and knowledge are wonderfully beyond human reach, inviting reverence and trust in His sovereign wisdom. This aligns with the biblical portrayal of God as one whose works and purposes are marvelous and hidden, calling believers to faith in His perfect and mysterious providence. Recognizing this helps believers embrace humility and awe before the divine, deepening their relationship with God who is both known and yet wonderfully secret.
keyVerseReflection: In Judges 13:18, the angel of the LORD responds, 'Why askest thou thus after my name, seeing it is secret?' Here, פִּלְאִי conveys that the angel's name is not only hidden but carries a sense of wonder that is beyond human grasp. This word enriches the verse by emphasizing the profound mystery surrounding divine identity, reminding us that some aspects of God's nature and revelation remain purposely veiled, encouraging faith rather than mere curiosity.
